Case report 
A healthy man aged 33 years had a tick bite in the left lower 
quadrant of the abdomen with no erythema 9 weeks before 
admission to our hospital. One week later he began to suffer 
from nocturnal pain in the left leg. From the 3rd week follow- 
ing the tick bite he experienced gradually increasing stiffness 
of the left calf and later also the thigh. He was aware of no 
sensory or motor deficits. The week prior to admission he de- 
veloped severe painful cramps of the leg muscles which occur- 
red spontaneously and could be elicited by loud noises. He oc- 
casionally completely lost control of his left leg and fell twice 
and hurt himself.

On admission, the patient was unable to walk without sup- 
port because of painful cramps and stiffness of the left leg ex- 
tensor muscles. During examination, spasmodic jerks in the 
left leg appeared either spontaneously or following voluntary 
movements, touch of either leg or even noises like shutting the 
door. Cranial nerve deficits, neck stiffness and back pain were 
absent. Coordination and sensation were normal, as was mus- 
cle strength in all limbs. No abnormalities of the deep tendon 
reflexes were seen except for an exaggerated ankle jerk on 
both sides and spontaneous as well as reflex myoclonus (in- 
duced, for example, by loud noise, touching or spraying the 
skin, taps to the leg tendons or even the bed) in his left leg. No 
pathological reflexes were observed.

Lumbar puncture disclosed elevated cell counts and pro- 
tein values (see Table 1) in the CSF. A magnetic resonance 
scan showed no abnormalities of brain or spinal cord either 
with or without gadolinium enhancement. 
Laboratory findings were also normal except creatine 
kinase levels of 878 units/1 dropping to normal (77 units/1) 1 
week after initiation of therapy. No dehydration, metabolic 
disturbances or electrolyte imbalance were observed. Weste> 
gren sedimentation rate was t5/32 mm. Serological testing for 
influenza A and B, parainfluenza, mumps, herpes simplex, 
varicella zoster, HIV I, coxsackie and echo viruses was nega- 
tive, as were assays for antibodies specfic for Listeria, syphilis 
and toxoplasmosis. The results of testing for antibodies to 
B. burgdorferi are given in Table 1. 
Therapy with 20 × 106 units/day penicillin G i.v. for 14 
days was initiated. The patient also received 500 units of poly- 
valent human anti-tetanus antibodies i.m. (Behringwerke, 
Marburg, FRG) although localized tetanus was improbable 
because of the electrophysiological findings (see below). Dur- 
ing the following days the patient slowly improved. The jerks 
were not as severe as before treatment and could then onty be 
elicited by touching the affected leg or by a jolt to the bed, but 
no more by toud noise. However, walking was still markedly 
impaired. Therapeutic trials with antispastic drugs showed 
moderate amelioration of cramps and ability to walk with 
tizanidine 3×6mg/day and baclofen 3x5mglday, but 
diazepam 3 x 5 mg/day was much more effective. 
Eight weeks after the onset of symptoms, the patient was 
still not able to walk distances greater than a few hundred 
metres without muscle cramps in the left leg. Three months 
later, the patient had no further difficulty in walking. No jerks 
had been noted during the previous 4 weeks. The only impair- 
ment left was slight difficulty in taking more than two steps on 
a staircase. Tendon reflexes of both legs were brisk with a pre- 
dominance in the left leg. Babinski's sign was now positive on 
both sides, more prominent on the left. 
CSF analysis 
Routine CSF studies revealed elevated protein and immuno- 
globulin values and a lymphocytic pleocytosis with 240 
leucoytes/~tl (see Table 1). The raised quotients for albumin 
and IgG indicated both a disruption of the blood-brain barrier 
and intrathecal synthesis of IgG at the first lumbar puncture.

Electromyographic analysis 
Several electromygraphic (EMG) examinations revealed a 
tonic firing of normal motor units in the left leg muslces which 
could not be suppressed voluntarily, but no denervation activ- 
ity or fasciculations. No abnormalities of sensory or motor 
nerve conduction velocities or sensory evoked potentials were 
seen. The mean latencies of the left patella and Achilles ten- 
don reflexes were found at 18 and 34ms, respectively. The 
post-reflex silent period in the left rectus femoris and gastro- 
cnemius muscles ranged between 96 and 122 ms (normal). 
EMG analysis of reflex myoclonus was performed by 
means of simultaneous EMG recordings from various leg mus- 
cles after supramaximal electrical stimulation (single shock, 
pulse width 0.2 ms) to the median or tibial nerves at the wrist 
or ankle, respectively. Reflex myoclonus constisted of a syn- 
chronized burst response and a long-lasting (up to 1.5 s) de- 
crescendo activity in all muscles recorded from, both compo- 
nents often being separated by a short (20-70ms) pause 
(Fig. 2). Onset latencies of the initial burst ranged between 31 
and 48 ms (mean: 41 ms) with ipsilateral tibial nerve stimula- 
tion. With contralateral tibial and ipsilateral median nerve 
stimulation the early burst in the same muscles occurred at 
latencies between 78 and 111 (mean: 88) or 74 to 95 ms (mean: 
78), respectively.

The patient described hefe presented with symptoms not pre- 
viously reported in neuroborreliosis. Clinically, his disease 
may be characterized as a partial stift man syndrome with 
muscle rigidity and painful myoclonic jerks confined to the left 
lower leg. The spasmodic jerks could even be elicited by 
noises or touch and were so severe that creatine kinase levels 
rose up to 10-fold normal. Local tetanus was initially consid- 
ered, but unlikely with normal silent periods in the affected 
leg. EMG analysis of reflex jerks after tibial nerve stimulation 
revealed onset latencies compatible with a probably disinhi- 
bited segmental oligosynaptic reflex path [11]. With both 
contralateral tibial as well as with median nerve stimulation 
such short reflex pathways were apparently not involved. 
However, the onset latencies of reflex myoclonus with the lat- 
ter stimulus sites were in the same range which gives some 
clue to the structures involved in reflex myoclonus transmis- 
sion. If supraspinal structures such as the brain stern or the 
sensorimotor cortex were involved, the reflex path to the 
target motoneurons in the lumbosacral cord would be defi- 
nitely longer (about 80-100 cm) with tibial than with median 
nerve stimulation; if only the lower spinal cord is involved, the 
total reflex path lengths from both stimulus sites to the target 
motoneurons are about equal. The overlap of the reflex myo- 
clonus latencies with tibial and median nerve stimulation in 
the present case suggests a spinal rather than a supraspinal re- 
flex myoclonus transmission. Thus, the clinical and neuro- 
physiological findings fit in with a spinal localization. As there 
was no evidence for an involvement of the long ascending and 
descending tracts, the process might be tentatively considered 
to be within the spinal grey matter. Indeed, stiffness and 
superimposed spasms are the prominent symptoms of disor-

ders predominantly affecting the small neurons within the spi- 
nal grey matter [8, 19]. 
The clinical picture of this patient showed some re- 
semblance to the stift man syndrome. However, it was con- 
fined to one leg and its infectious origin was confirmed by CSF 
findings, positive serology and the demonstration of intrathec- 
ally produced, oligoclonal, B. burgdorferi-specific IgG bands. 
These bands clearly show that specific antibodies are locally 
produced and are probably the best indicator for the aetiolog- 
ical relevante of B. burgdorferi. In patients with B. burgdor- 
feri radiculomyelitis, it has been demonstrated that these anti- 
bodies are persistently secreted within the CSF [9]. The pa- 
tient described here was treated intravenously with penicillin 
G 20 x 106 units/day for 14 days. Both his symptoms and the 
CSF findings subsequently improved during the following 
weeks. 
Earlier reports have suggested an infectious origin in cases 
with subacute myoclonic spinal neuronitis closely resembling 
stift man syndrome [5, 8, 19]. Only recently has it been dem- 
onstrated that the latter syndrome may be related to auto- 
antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase [18]. The agent 
involved in this patient's disease, B. burgdorferi, is able to in- 
duce autoreactive T cells and autoantibodies specific for brain 
antigens [10, 14, 17]. Therefore, the spinal cord disturbances 
could have been mediated either by the spirochaete itself or 
by the above-mentioned autoimmune process. Although the 
true nature and target structure of this localized myelitis can- 
not be determined with certainty by the techniques used here, 
the present case provides evidence for a link between a clinical 
entity with a still unknown aetiology as well as localization and 
a defined infectious agent, B. burgdorferi.
